title: Hash Index
description: Trace equality buckets and collisions, scope expected lookup costs, and distinguish hash range limits, composite probes and MySQL engine capabilities.

questions.question_text: What does a hash index use to determine where a value's pointer is stored?
options: A sorted comparison against other keys
A hash function that maps the value directly to a bucket/location
The physical order of the table's rows
questions.explanation: A hash function computes a bucket number directly from the value, without any sorted comparisons.

questions.question_text: Under suitable hash distribution and load assumptions, what is the simplified expected exact-bucket lookup complexity?
questions.explanation: ExpectedO(1) describes a model of bucket access, not a worst-case or full-query latency guarantee.

questions.question_text: Which predicate cannot generally use the hash index as an ordered range-navigation path?
options: Both A and B cannot be supported
questions.explanation: BETWEEN can still execute through another access path; the hash structure does not preserve the ordered interval.

questions.question_text: Why can't a hash index support `ORDER BY` on the indexed column?
options: ORDER BY is not valid SQL syntax
The hash function scrambles values so that similar values do not end up stored near each other
Hash indexes do not allow duplicate values
Hash indexes are always slower than B+ Trees
questions.explanation: Since hashing intentionally destroys any relationship between nearby values, there's no way to derive sorted order from bucket positions.

questions.question_text: Which scenario is the best candidate for a hash index?
options: A column frequently queried with ORDER BY
A column used exclusively for exact-match lookups, like an opaque session token, never for ranges or sorting
A column used mainly in BETWEEN range filters
A column that needs to support LIKE 'prefix%' matching
questions.explanation: A complete exact-match workload can suit hashing when the engine and persistence requirements support it. This is not a recommendation to store real authentication secrets in an unreviewed MEMORY fixture.

questions.question_text: What must a hash index's implementation handle when two different values hash to the same bucket?
options: Nothing; this situation is impossible by design
Hash collisions, typically via chaining within a bucket
The database automatically drops one of the values
questions.explanation: Collisions are a normal part of hashing and are handled internally (e.g., via chained entries within a bucket).

questions.question_text: Why do many database engines default to B-Tree/B+ Tree indexes rather than hash indexes for general-purpose columns?
options: Because hash indexes are always slower for equality lookups too
Because most real query workloads eventually need range queries or sorting on the same column, which hash indexes cannot serve
Because hash indexes cannot be created at all in most engines
Because B-Trees use less storage than hash indexes in every case
questions.explanation: Ordered tree structures support equality and ordered-range opportunities. Whether either access method is faster depends on the actual engine, distribution, maintenance and workload.

questions.question_text: A composite hash index is built over (department, gpa). What kind of query can it typically serve?
options: A range query on department alone
An exact-match query specifying both department and gpa together
A sort by gpa within each department
questions.explanation: Hash indexes over multiple columns generally only support exact-match equality on the full combination, unlike a composite B+ Tree index's leftmost-prefix support.

questions.question_text: What additional step follows choosing a collision bucket?
options: Assume every entry is the same key
questions.explanation: Hash routing finds candidates; logical equality identifies matches.

questions.question_text: In key mod 4, which bucket contains 13?
questions.explanation: Thirteen has remainder one on division by four.

questions.question_text: Can 9 and 13 coexist in the same bucket without being duplicate keys?
questions.explanation: A hash collision is distinct from logical key equality.

questions.question_text: What does expected constant-time navigation not guarantee?
options: A candidate bucket can be found
A hash function computes a result
questions.explanation: Row fetches, collisions, output and concurrency add costs.

questions.question_text: Does inability to use a hash range path make BETWEEN invalid SQL?
questions.explanation: The engine can execute the query through another path.

questions.question_text: Does bucket order imply natural key order?
questions.explanation: Hash mapping does not preserve ordered key neighborhoods.

questions.question_text: What must a fair access-method benchmark preserve?
options: Required data semantics, persistence and workload conditions
questions.explanation: Changing engine durability or workload makes results incomparable.

questions.question_text: Is InnoDB adaptive hashing the same as declaring arbitrary userHASH indexes on InnoDB columns?
options: Only if the column is text
questions.explanation: An internal mechanism and a declared engine-specific index are different capabilities.

questions.question_text: What can make an equality bucket expensive?
questions.explanation: Fast routing does not make a large result population free.

questions.question_text: What does a typical composite hash probe require?
options: The complete indexed tuple’s equality values
Only any one component by default
An ORDER BY clause instead of values
questions.explanation: Full-tuple hashing differs from ordered left-prefix navigation.

questions.question_text: What affects textual key equality in SQL?
questions.explanation: Index routing must remain consistent with logical comparison rules.

questions.question_text: Which changes can require index maintenance?
options: Inserts, deletes and updates to indexed keys
questions.explanation: Read performance must be evaluated alongside write maintenance.

notes:
## Route an equality lookup to a candidate bucket

A hash index applies a hash function to a search key and uses the result to locate a bucket of candidate entries. It is designed primarily for exact equality lookup. Unlike an ordered tree, it does not arrange neighboring keys in their natural comparison order. Understanding this distinction helps explain why an index can be useful for locating one exact identifier while offering no ordered range path for nearby identifiers.

Consider a synthetic session registry queried by an exact opaque identifier. The application is not asking for all identifiers between two textual bounds or for identifiers sorted alphabetically. A hash-oriented access path can suit that pattern when the chosen storage engine supports it. The index remains a physical lookup structure; it does not validate session authority, protect secret values or replace application expiration and ownership rules.

## Trace hashing without confusing it with equality

For a tiny teaching model, let bucket number equal the integer key modulo four. Keys 9 and 13 both map to bucket 1, while 10 maps to bucket 2. Looking for 13 first selects bucket 1, then compares the actual candidate keys so9 is not incorrectly returned. Different keys sharing a bucket demonstrate a collision, not proof that they are equal or that one entry should replace the other.

| Key | Teaching hash: key mod 4 | Candidate bucket |
|---|---|---|
| 9 | 1 | Bucket 1 |
| 13 | 1 | Bucket 1 |
| 10 | 2 | Bucket 2 |
| 20 | 0 | Bucket 0 |

Real implementations use more sophisticated hashing and bucket management. The simple modulo formula is a transparent exercise, not a recommendation for an engine's production hash function. A good explanation separates routing from final key comparison. It also distinguishes a hash index collision from a primary-key or unique-constraint violation: colliding unequal keys can coexist if the logical uniqueness rule permits them.

## Understand average-case cost and its assumptions

A simplified well-managed hash table can offer expected constant-time bucket access for an exact lookup under suitable distribution and load assumptions. This does not mean every database request has constant latency. The bucket can contain several entries, the key can be expensive to hash or compare, and the query can need additional row reads and visibility checks. Returning many duplicates also costs work proportional to the qualifying population.

Skewed keys, high load or repeated values can make a bucket expensive. Resizing or reorganizing the structure can add maintenance cost. Memory pressure, caching and concurrent access add further implementation-dependent effects. The average-case model is useful for explaining navigation, but it is not a benchmark result or a guarantee that hash access beats every B+ tree on a real workload.

## Explain why range navigation is missing

An ordered tree can locate a lower bound and continue through neighboring ordered entries. Hash routing has no corresponding natural-order guarantee. Keys close numerically or textually can map to unrelated buckets, while distant keys can collide. A BETWEEN condition or inequality therefore cannot generally use the hash structure as an ordered interval path in the way an appropriate B-tree index can.

The query can still execute by another access path, such as scanning rows or using another index. Saying a hash index does not support ordered range navigation is not saying that SQL BETWEEN becomes illegal. Likewise, an equality IN list can sometimes be treated as several exact probes under an engine's supported rules. Separate query validity, optimizer choices and the specific access opportunity the index provides.

## Keep ORDER BY as an output contract

A hash index does not supply the indexed values in natural sorted order. A query requiring ORDER BY key needs another plan component or suitable ordered access path. An accidental small-fixture output sequence is not a promise. Bucket numbering itself also does not sort the original keys, as the 9/13 collision and 20 example demonstrate.

Even a B-tree scan should not be treated as an implicit SQL output-order guarantee when ORDER BY is absent. The statement must express the required ordering. The structure explains one possible implementation strategy; the query contract tells the reader which result order is required. This distinction avoids teaching a physical coincidence as a stable application interface.

## Distinguish MySQL engines and internal mechanisms

MySQL index capabilities depend on the storage engine. MEMORY supports HASH and BTREE choices for relevant indexes, and its durability and operational behavior differ from an InnoDB table. Do not move persistent application data into MEMORY merely to obtain a hash example. The educational syntax belongs in an isolated fixture with an explicitly appropriate lifetime and no real credentials or private session identifiers.

```sql
CREATE TABLE hash_lookup_lab (
  item_id INT NOT NULL,
  label VARCHAR(40),
  INDEX item_lookup USING HASH (item_id)
) ENGINE=MEMORY;
```

InnoDB also has an adaptive hash mechanism associated with its own execution internals. That is not equivalent to an application declaring an arbitrary user HASH index on an InnoDB column. Its use and cost depend on implementation and workload. Check the documented engine and version rather than treating every occurrence of the word hash in a plan or configuration as the same schema feature.

## Inspect composite-key requirements

A composite hash key typically hashes the complete indexed tuple. An equality lookup supplying both department and grade can select its complete key bucket. Supplying only department does not generally offer the same ordered leftmost-prefix navigation as a composite B-tree. The engine may choose another access path, but the complete-tuple hash structure alone should not be described as a range of departments followed by grades.

NULL support, collation and equality semantics depend on the engine and indexed types. Two textual spellings that compare equal under the chosen collation must be treated consistently with the index's comparison contract. Do not reason from raw byte differences alone when predicting a SQL equality match. The physical hash routing and the logical equality rules must work together.

## Include duplicates and maintenance in the decision

A nonunique equality value can return many records. Finding the bucket quickly does not remove the cost of locating and returning every qualifying row. If most rows share one status value, a hash index on status can still leave a large result population. An exact opaque identifier and a highly repeated status are both equality predicates but have very different selectivity and output costs.

INSERT, DELETE and key-changing UPDATE operations maintain the index. A benchmark that measures only warm-cache point reads misses those costs and can choose poorly for a write-heavy system. Compare representative reads, writes, memory use and concurrency conditions. Keep data integrity and required persistence behavior fixed while comparing access methods; an incomparable engine conversion is not a fair index-only experiment.

## Record a plan experiment reproducibly

For a disposable comparison, record table definitions, index types, row count, value distribution and exact query parameters. Inspect the chosen access path rather than assuming that creating an index forces the optimizer to use it. Repeat under representative warm and cold conditions where appropriate, and keep the result semantics identical. A query returning the right row establishes correctness of that result, but not that the expected hash probe occurred. A plan showing a probe establishes an access choice for those conditions, but not a universal speed ranking across all later workloads.

## Solve two bucket and workload exercises

First exercise: using key mod 4, place 9, 13, 10 and 20 into buckets, then search for 13 and 17. The solution compares keys inside bucket 1, finds 13 and reports 17 absent even though 17 selects the same bucket. Explain why the collision does not justify returning 9 and why uniqueness would still compare the actual logical key.

Second exercise: choose between an exact full-key lookup, a request for keys 100 through 200, and a report sorted by key. The hash structure supplies a natural opportunity only for the complete equality lookup; the other requirements need a different path or additional work. Add a composite department-grade key and explain why specifying only department is not a complete hash probe. Continue with [B+ trees](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/b-plus-tree), [composite indexes](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/composite-index) and [selectivity](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/selectivity) to evaluate access paths by their actual supported operations.
